Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. In March 1908 the Hope family crossed the Atlantic from England to Cleveland, Ohio. source
  2. Among the seven sons was a four-year-old named Leslie Townes Hope. source
  3. His father's first job there was carving stone for the Church of the Covenant, and he later worked on Cleveland's Guardians of Traffic. source
  4. The boy went to the Fairmount schools and East High, sang in the Church of the Covenant choir, took dancing lessons, and boxed briefly under the name "Packy East" before losing in a novice championship and giving it up. source
  5. Hope went into vaudeville in 1922, worked up through partner acts and Broadway revues, and in 1928 struck out as a solo comedian — changing his first name to "Bob." source
  6. Hollywood made him a star. source
  7. He took his radio show overseas in 1943, began his Christmas shows for the troops in 1948, and performed for American servicemen and women through the Korean War, Vietnam, and the Gulf War. source
  8. In 1997 the House of Representatives made him the first civilian ever named an honorary veteran of the United States armed forces. source
  9. Hope never took a citizenship oath of his own. source
  10. Under the law of the time, a child became a citizen automatically when a parent was naturalised. source
  11. As the record plainly states: source
  12. When his father was naturalized in December 1920, Hope became a United States citizen.
  13. He was seventeen. source
  14. The boy who had crossed the Atlantic at four was made an American by an act in which he took no part. source
  15. This is the citation read out when he received his second Honorary Award: source
  16. To Bob Hope for unique and distinguished service to our industry and the Academy. source
  17. Is a citizen made by a ceremony, or by the life a person lives in a country?
